rv.q: This remains a landmark play in British drama; and, if men should weep, it is because Lamont Stewart was discouraged from ever writing a successor to a work that blends such indignation with theatrical exuberance.
Performed by a superbly marshalled cast, Rourke's production avoids any trace of melodrama, the actors revelling in the demotic poetry of the stingingly humorous Glaswegian dialect.
The director, Josie Rourke, has given us a sincere and honourable version, but Men Should Weep still feels like an overlong and distinctly overrated play.

Admittedly these snippets don’t have the “lived” intensity you might expect in a full “Lower Depths” treatment, nor does the production carry the emotional weight or poetic beauty of Giles Haveregal’s 7:84 revival (there’s an awful lot of “shouty” shouting, and the wigs are abysmal; why do they bother?).
If this is meant to be a picture of real people in a real slum then the evening is an utter failure.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this National Theatre revival of Stewart's 1930s Glasgow tenement drama, with some praising its rich depiction of working-class struggle and others finding it lacking in authenticity and dramatic power.
